title: The Twenty-Five Tales of the Vetala
description: This episode retells the Baital Pachisi, the Sanskrit frame story in which King Vikramaditya must silently carry a corpse-possessing spirit through a graveyard, only to lose it each time he answers one of its riddles correctly. It lays out who Vikrama, the vetala, and the treacherous holy man actually are, and how the twenty-fifth unanswerable riddle sets up the king's final betrayal and triumph.

turns.speaker: narrator
turns.text: This is a story collected in India sometime around a thousand years ago, about a king named Vikrama who gets talked into carrying a corpse through a graveyard at night.

turns.speaker: narrator
turns.text: [serious] A holy man asks Vikrama to fetch a body hanging upside down from a tree, so it can be used in a ritual. Vikrama climbs up, cuts it down, and slings it over his shoulder, and the moment he starts walking, the corpse starts talking. Living inside it is a vetala, a spirit that inhabits dead bodies and tells stories, and it offers the king a deal. It will tell him a tale that ends in a riddle. If Vikrama knows the answer and stays silent, his head will burst into pieces. If he gets the answer wrong, the vetala will let itself be carried the rest of the way.

turns.speaker: narrator
turns.text: But if Vikrama answers correctly, out loud, the vetala flies straight back to its tree, and the king has to start all over again, walking into the dark to cut it down a second time.

turns.speaker: narrator
turns.text: [wry] And here is the trap built into the whole thing. Vikrama always knows the answer. Every single story ends with a question he cannot pretend not to understand, and the rule says that knowing and staying quiet kills him, so he has no choice but to speak, and the moment he speaks, he loses the body all over again. This happens twenty four times. Twenty four stories, twenty four riddles, twenty four times the corpse goes flying back up into its tree and Vikrama walks back into the graveyard to fetch it down once more.

turns.speaker: narrator
turns.text: [slowly] On the twenty fifth telling, the vetala gives him a riddle about a father and son who each marry a mother and daughter from the same family, and the children born afterward, and what those two children are to each other. It is the one question that finally stops the king cold. He does not know the answer.

turns.speaker: narrator
turns.text: [quietly] Satisfied, the vetala lets itself be carried all the way to the holy man without a single trick. But on the road there, it tells the king one more thing, unasked. The holy man plans to kill him during the ritual, bowing before the goddess, to seize the vetala's power for himself.

turns.speaker: narrator
turns.text: [grim] The vetala tells Vikrama exactly how to turn the bow into a killing stroke of his own. Vikrama does it, beheads the holy man first, and the goddess he was bowing to grants the king a reward instead, the vetala's loyalty, ready to help him whenever he calls.

turns.speaker: narrator
turns.text: The king spent the entire night losing a game he could never actually win, and that was the only way to reach the one night he needed to.

turns.speaker: narrator
turns.text: There are a lot more of these where that came from, so follow along if you want them. See you next time.
